summary: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) promises specific guarantees, such as very low loss and bounded latency and jitter, so it needs security beyond usual best practice. This informational document covers threats and attacks, how they relate to use cases and service properties, and component-level protections such as ingress filtering and detecting packets that arrive at the wrong time. It also covers the IP and MPLS data planes.

plainLanguage.summary: A network that promises packets always arrive on time needs extra guards, since a bully who delays a few could ruin everything. This document lists the dangers and how to guard against them.

questions: how do you attack a deterministic network
why is timing important in detnet security
subtitle: Protecting networks that guarantee delivery speed and reliability.

tldr.problem: Deterministic networks promise extremely fast, reliable delivery for critical applications like power grids and industrial control. Those guarantees become targets: an attacker that delays even a few packets can disable the entire system.
tldr.mechanism: This document catalogs threats specific to DetNet (delay attacks, flow spoofing, resource exhaustion, synchronization attacks), analyzes their impact on different use cases, and describes mitigation strategies such as path redundancy, integrity protection, and timing violation detection.
tldr.outcome: Complements the DetNet architecture specifications with security guidance for system and component designers, recognizing that the broad range of DetNet use cases requires flexible security measures rather than one-size-fits-all prescriptions.

today: RFC 9055 is an informational document that complements the DetNet architecture specifications (RFC 8655 and related data-plane RFCs). It has not been obsoleted and provides the definitive security guidance for DetNet implementations.

sections.title: DetNet: Speed and Reliability as a Service
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) brings to IP networks what was previously limited to isolated operational-technology systems: the ability to guarantee that specific flows of data will arrive with extremely low loss and bounded latency—including tight limits on latency variation (jitter). This is indispensable for real-time applications like power-grid automation, industrial machinery control, and building management.

The security challenge is that DetNet breaks the isolation. OT networks traditionally sat behind air-gapped firewalls. DetNet merges IT and OT traffic on the same network, exposing critical control systems to attackers who now have access to wide-area IP infrastructure. A classical network security tool—throttling traffic to prevent denial-of-service—becomes useless when the SLA requires microsecond delivery windows. The design challenge is to defend DetNet flows without breaking the timing guarantees that justify the network's existence.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet is like a conveyor belt that promises to deliver packages in exactly 2 seconds, every time. Old factories had locked warehouses nobody could reach. Now the conveyor goes across town where anyone can touch it. You need new guards that check packages without slowing them down.

sections.title: Core DetNet Concepts
sections.content:
DetNet systems rely on three key techniques. Resource allocation reserves bandwidth and buffer space at intermediate routers, so one DetNet flow cannot starve another. Explicit routes constrain path choices to avoid reroutes that would exceed latency bounds. Packet Replication and Elimination (PREOF) sends the same packet along multiple paths and discards duplicates at the destination, giving redundancy without losing the timing guarantees.

The security premise is that these resources are inviolable: no other traffic—malicious or accidental—can consume them. This assumption is critical for threat analysis. If a compromised node can inject packets into a DetNet flow's resource budget, then all the analysis falls apart. Conversely, a network with perfect resource isolation can survive attacks that would cripple a best-effort network.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet uses three tricks: reserve a lane just for priority traffic so it doesn't get stuck behind cars; nail down the route so the truck always takes the same road; and send duplicate packages on different roads so if one gets lost, you have a backup. The trick only works if nobody sneaks into the reserved lane.

sections.title: Threats and Attacks
sections.content:
The RFC classifies attackers along two axes: internal (with network access or encryption keys) vs. external (outside the DetNet perimeter), and on-path (able to intercept packets) vs. off-path (can only send new packets). The threats fall into categories.

Delay attacks hold up packets to miss their time windows, disrupting real-time control loops. A 3 ms latency SLA that receives a 5 ms packet may cause physical damage in a controlled system. Flow modification and spoofing alter headers so packets are misrouted, or inject fake packets that consume the flow's bandwidth allocation. Resource segmentation attacks exploit shared buffers or processing queues to exhaust resources needed for DetNet flows. Time-synchronization attacks poison the clock that DetNet relies on for scheduling and PREOF elimination decisions.

The RFC also catalogs impact by use case: a delay attack on an electrical utility has high criticality because failure affects public safety and recovery is slow. An industrial machine control loop failure might only affect one organization.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers can delay your package so you miss the deadline. They can disguise a fake package as real one. They can jam up the loading dock so real packages are dropped. Or they can mess with the clock so the system doesn't know when things arrive. Some tricks are scary for power plants, others just annoying for factories.

sections.title: Defenses Against Attacks
sections.content:
The RFC presents a toolkit of mitigations that system designers can apply based on their threat model. Path redundancy using PREOF mitigates on-path attacks by delivering over multiple paths. An attacker controlling one path cannot disrupt the flow. Integrity protection uses message authentication codes (MACs) to detect packet modification at intermediate nodes; the cost is latency overhead that must fit within the SLA.

DetNet node authentication verifies that control-plane messages come from authorized nodes, preventing spoofed instructions. Synthetic traffic insertion mixes fake packets into the traffic stream to mask real packet timing, defeating passive reconnaissance. Dynamic performance analytics monitors for timing and bandwidth violations and triggers action (dropping the offending traffic, alerting the controller, or locating the attack source).

The document is not prescriptive: it presents the available tools and leaves system designers to choose based on use case. A low-cost system may accept higher risk; a utility-scale network must be hardened more thoroughly.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send backups on different roads. You can seal packages so thieves can't repackage them. You can require drivers to show ID. You can mix in fake packages to confuse spies. You can watch for signs of trouble and react fast. Pick the defenses that match your risk.

sections.title: Component Designer Responsibilities
sections.content:
Beyond system-level mitigations, the designers of DetNet routers and switches must ensure that their components enforce inviolable resource isolation. This means implementing ingress policing to block traffic that exceeds allocated bandwidth before it enters the DetNet domain. It means documenting which security properties the component provides (integrity checks on flow IDs, sequence number protection, etc.) so system integrators know what they can rely on.

When a packet arrives outside its expected time window or with a bandwidth violation, the component must detect it and take action: dropping it, logging the event, or signaling the controller. Choosing the right response is application-specific; a crude response (like shutting down the interface) might harm the protected system more than the attacker's packet.

The underlying principle is that the security of the network is only as strong as its weakest link. A resource-constrained device designed for cost may not be suitable for a critical utility network. Responsibility falls on the system designer to select components appropriate to their security requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The package loader must check that no one overloads the truck before it leaves the depot. The driver's manual should say whether packages are sealed and how. When weird packages show up, the driver needs to know whether to throw them out, report them, or ask the boss. Every weak link matters, so you have to be honest about what's protected and what isn't.
